rows.practice: applies suitable research methods to housing questions, builds evidence-based answers to housing problems and involves residents, seldom-heard groups included, in decisions about their homes
rows.knowledge: how housing problems arise and how law and policy have answered them, with the core principles of housing economics, finance and the governance of housing organisations
rows.identity: a housing professional in training who sees the home as central to residents' well-being and takes professional responsibility for equality, diversity and inclusion in housing services

rows.practice: compares housing systems across the UK and abroad, transfers good practice where it fits and devises alternative solutions, environmental ones included, that act on structural inequality
rows.knowledge: a critical and self-aware grasp of housing policy, development, finance and management (above all quickly shifting fields like digital technology) and of lessons from health and criminal justice
rows.identity: a confident, reflective practitioner who challenges the decisions of any housing stakeholder, knows the limits of their own competence and works ethically and resiliently as conditions change

rows.practice: evaluates current housing research and advanced scholarship, locates where evidence on housing problems runs out and produces new insight for housing policy and professional practice
rows.knowledge: housing knowledge across policy, finance, governance and sustainability held at the leading edge of research and professional practice, with an understanding of how research moves it on
rows.identity: a self-directing housing scholar-practitioner who leads their own academic and professional development and answers for the new insight they bring to the sector (ing's reading)

digest.definition: A field of study, interdisciplinary since the early 1980s, that starts from a household's basic need for a home in which to live well and flourish
distinctiveFeatures: A field of study, interdisciplinary since the early 1980s, that starts from a household's basic need for a home in which to live well and flourish
It links home, dwellings and neighbourhoods with the institutions and actors that provide housing, across market and social sectors, judged by adequacy, affordability and security
It draws on the social sciences, law, health, geography, planning, surveying, construction, architecture and management; it applies theory to practical situations
It is vocational and functional: knowledge that can be applied, with a three-fold design joining behaviours and values, skills and knowledge, shaped by the CIH's professional standards
It sees itself as a subject of social justice, attentive to rights, homelessness and the lived experience of housing, including students' own
Its courses reflect devolved housing law, policy and governance across the four UK nations
Students arrive by many routes, often already working in housing; recognition of prior learning, part-time study and employer partnerships are characteristic

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: framed as social justice: housing rights, disadvantage, intersectional inequality, class and tenure stigma and the most vulnerable groups as content; an inclusive curriculum that recognises students may have known housing precarity; inclusive behaviours for graduates (D1, 1.12 to 1.19); also in content and the generic skills (D1, 3.1, 4.8)

built on the UN SDGs, with SDG 11 and target 11.1 on adequate, safe and affordable housing at the centre; UNESCO's eight competencies adapted for housing; the campus and community as a living laboratory (D1, 1.20 to 1.30); repeated in delivery and in the threshold and generic skills (D1, 3.14, 4.3, 4.8)

headed employability and enterprise education: a vocational subject whose entrepreneurship includes social entrepreneurship, careers across public, private and third sectors, placements and the reflective, resilient practitioner (D1, 1.31 to 1.35); work experience through employer partnerships (D1, 2.15)

accessible environments, materials and site visits for students with learning or mobility needs and for those disadvantaged by structural inequality; content designed so lived experience of housing problems is not a barrier (D1, 2.5, 2.6); adjustments in teaching and assessment (D1, 3.7, 3.20)

subjectSpecific.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to spot housing problems, including environmental and sustainability ones, and come up with different ways to solve them.

transferable.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to work on your own and with others to spot complex problems and pull together what is already known about a topic.
By the end of your degree, you will be able to take charge of your learning, show you grasp the ideas, make sound judgements and explain your ideas well to different people.
By the end of your degree, you will be able to work with others, including people from other professions, in assessed and unassessed tasks, as you will in housing work.
By the end of your degree, you will be able to show that you understand issues of equality, diversity and inclusion and that you take professional responsibility for acting on them.
By the end of your degree, you will be able to use a range of software to gather and assess information and data from different sources.
By the end of your degree, you will be able to reflect on and manage your own learning and personal growth, and how you act ethically and professionally.
By the end of your degree, you will be able to think about what you have learned and use it to make yourself more employable and enterprising for the career you want.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree
Characteristics of a Housing Studies degree

statements.appliesTo: Housing Studies courses across the UK
statements.about: differences between the four nations
statements.paraphrase: Courses will reflect global, national and devolved governance and will need to allow for how housing law, policy and governance, and the housing bodies, differ between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, even though the CIH itself works UK-wide.

forPractitioner.text: Plan content so that it will take account of how housing law, policy and governance differ between the four nations, and of the different housing bodies in each, rather than teaching one nation's system as the UK model.

forBeneficiary.text: You will learn how housing law, policy and governance differ between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and which housing bodies work in each.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree

statements.appliesTo: teaching and learning in housing studies
statements.about: an inclusive curriculum grounded in social justice
statements.paraphrase: Because housing studies is about social justice, its teaching will centre on an inclusive curriculum that recognises how varied learners are, including that some may have lived through housing precarity, and that invites students to question decisions in policy and practice.

forPractitioner.text: Put an inclusive curriculum at the centre of teaching: assume some students may have known housing precarity at first hand, draw on the many policy networks the subject touches and encourage students to challenge decisions made in policy and in practice.

forBeneficiary.text: You will study in a curriculum built around inclusion and social justice, one that recognises that you or others in your group may have lived through housing insecurity and that encourages you to challenge decisions in policy and practice.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree

statements.about: confidence to engage and challenge stakeholders
statements.paraphrase: Graduates will build the self-reflection and confidence to work strategically, collaboratively and critically with stakeholders in policy, practice and other disciplines, and will have been helped to challenge the decisions of any stakeholder with housing expertise.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will leave able to reflect on themselves and to engage stakeholders across policy, practice and other disciplines strategically, collaboratively and critically; design support that lets them practise challenging decisions with housing knowledge behind them.

forBeneficiary.text: You will develop the self-awareness and confidence to work with people across policy, practice and other disciplines, strategically and critically, and to challenge their decisions using what you know about housing.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree
Sustainability: developing sustainable development knowledge in housing studies

statements.about: courses directed at the SDGs' concerns
statements.paraphrase: In line with the SDGs set by UN member states in 2015, Housing Studies courses should be directed towards tackling social, economic and environmental concerns for a better world.

forPractitioner.text: Orient the course towards the social, economic and environmental concerns behind the 17 SDGs, so that its purpose is visible in module aims and content.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course design; the student meets it through the curriculum

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree
Sustainability: developing sustainable development knowledge in housing studies

statements.about: enough sustainability content for confident discussion
statements.paraphrase: Quality, accessible housing runs through several SDGs, SDG 11 above all, and housing can help meet the others (for example SDGs 1, 3, 5 and 7); the stated expectation is that courses hold enough sustainability content for students to be aware of the issues and confident discussing them in housing.

forPractitioner.text: Give the course enough sustainability content, tied to SDG 11 and to goals such as 1, 3, 5 and 7, that students can discuss sustainability in a housing context with knowledge and confidence.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect enough teaching on sustainability, such as the UN goal on sustainable cities and goals on poverty, health, gender equality and energy, to discuss it confidently in housing.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree

statements.appliesTo: course and module outcomes for ESD
statements.about: ESD outcomes linking knowledge, competencies and SDGs
statements.paraphrase: ESD learning outcomes at course and module level should link housing knowledge and skills with the sustainability competencies and the 17 SDGs; the stated expectation is that courses build the UNESCO competencies step by step and that assessment shows they are achieved.

forPractitioner.text: Write ESD outcomes that join housing knowledge and skills to the UNESCO sustainability competencies and the 17 SDGs; develop the competencies progressively across levels and make sure assessment evidences them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on outcome writing and assessment design; the student meets its effect

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition of the learning environment, provided by the course

Sustainability: developing learning environments to promote sustainable development

statements.about: learning spaces used as alternative locations
statements.paraphrase: ESD needs campus, outdoor and other learning spaces to be used to the full as places where students build and show its competencies.

forPractitioner.text: Use the campus, outdoor settings and other spaces as places where students develop and demonstrate sustainability competencies.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition of the learning environment, provided by the course

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree
Sustainability: developing learning environments to promote sustainable development

statements.about: the campus and community as a living laboratory
statements.paraphrase: Teaching, learning and assessment should use the opportunities the campus, the local community and online settings offer; treating campus and community as a living laboratory can give authentic housing learning, and the stated expectation is that courses use varied environments to build sustainability understanding and competencies.

forPractitioner.text: Use the campus, the local community and online spaces as settings for learning and assessment, for instance as a living laboratory for housing questions, so that students build sustainability understanding and competencies in more than one environment.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect some of your learning and assessment to happen on campus, in the local community or online, treating real places as a living laboratory for housing and sustainability.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree
Sustainability: developing learning environments to promote sustainable development

statements.appliesTo: curriculum design at course and module level
statements.about: sustainable development embedded in the curriculum
statements.paraphrase: To advance sustainable development, the agenda should be built into curriculum design at course and module level, with learning environments that let students gain the knowledge, understanding and skills to act towards sustainable futures and to link housing with health and education.

forPractitioner.text: Embed sustainable development in the design of both the course and its modules, and provide environments in which students build the knowledge and skills to act for sustainable communities and to connect housing with health and education.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on curriculum design; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree
Sustainability: developing learning environments to promote sustainable development

statements.about: ESD across content, teaching and assessment
statements.paraphrase: ESD should show in module content, teaching and learning methods, structure and delivery and assessment; inclusive, interdisciplinary approaches with recognised extra and co-curricular work are encouraged, and case studies, project research and visits to communities facing unsustainability can enrich learning.

forPractitioner.text: Make ESD visible in what modules teach, how they teach it, how they are structured and how they assess; use case studies, project-based research and community visits where symptoms of unsustainability show.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on module design; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree
Sustainability: developing learning environments to promote sustainable development

statements.appliesTo: ESD content and the subject area
statements.about: the focus of ESD content and learning environments
statements.paraphrase: ESD content should centre on keeping physical environments whole, on social justice and on economic development, drawing on diverse voices and other disciplines; the subject area should be able to build and strengthen environments, physical, virtual and digital, that promote sustainable development.

forPractitioner.text: Focus ESD content on physical environmental integrity, social justice and economic development, include under-represented voices and other disciplines, and keep improving physical and digital learning spaces for sustainability.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on content and learning environments; the student meets its effect

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree

statements.about: transferable, self-management and problem-solving skills
statements.paraphrase: Graduates will have transferable skills for present housing work and for new roles built on new technology; they will manage and motivate themselves and others, spot housing problems, own ideas and decisions to solve them, handle risk and know the limits of their professional competence and judgement.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will carry transferable skills into current and emerging housing roles: self-management and motivating others, identifying housing problems, taking responsibility for ideas and decisions, managing risk and recognising the bounds of their own professional judgement.

forBeneficiary.text: You will gain skills you can use in housing jobs now and in new roles that technology creates: managing yourself, motivating others, spotting housing problems, taking ownership of ideas and decisions, handling risk and knowing where your professional judgement stops.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Housing Studies degree

statements.about: professional knowledge, reflection, ethics and resilience
statements.paraphrase: Graduates will know housing well across policy, development, finance, management, research, sustainability and equality; reflect critically on their own knowledge, especially in fast-changing areas such as digital technology; direct their own learning and development; bring in good practice from neighbouring fields such as health and criminal justice; and work ethically, sensitively, resiliently and creatively, adapting as situations change.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will combine broad housing knowledge with reflective, self-directed professional development, transfer good practice from allied fields, act ethically with attention to equality and diversity and stay resilient and adaptable in a changing sector.

forBeneficiary.text: You will know housing broadly, from policy and finance to sustainability and equality; reflect on your own skills, especially as technology changes; take charge of your own development; borrow good practice from fields such as health; and work ethically, resiliently and creatively as things change.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Housing Studies degree

statements.appliesTo: learning environments, materials and site visits
statements.about: accessible learning environments and site visits
statements.paraphrase: Learning environments and materials should be accessible to students with a wide range of learning or mobility needs and to those whose prior learning was limited by structural inequality; all should be able to take full part, with adjustments and support where suitable, and site visits should be arranged so every student can attend.

forPractitioner.text: Design spaces, materials and site visits for students with learning, sensory or mobility needs and for those whose earlier education was limited by disadvantage; make adjustments in line with national frameworks and institutional services so that everyone can participate fully.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to take a full part in your course whatever your learning or mobility needs or your background, with adjustments and support where you need them, including on site visits.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Housing Studies degree

statements.about: lived experience in the content; flexible recruitment
statements.paraphrase: Every student has lived somewhere, and some have faced the housing problems the course teaches; course design can recognise this so that the content raises no barriers and students may share experience if they choose, and recruitment should be flexible enough for learners with little academic background but sector experience to flourish.

forPractitioner.text: Design content so that students who have faced housing problems are not put off by it and can choose to share their experience; recruit flexibly, for example through whole-person approaches, links with feeder providers and induction support in academic writing and critical thinking for non-traditional entrants.

forBeneficiary.text: If you have lived through housing problems yourself, the course should let you engage with that content safely and share your experience only if you wish; if you come from housing work rather than academic study, you should find a route in and support to start.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Housing Studies degree

statements.about: progression to the threshold across the honours levels
statements.paraphrase: Through an honours degree (FHEQ Level 6, FQHEIS Level 10) a student will move from level to level under institutional rules, each level building towards meeting every threshold subject-specific and generic skill; joint honours students will meet part of these and add others from their second subject.

forPractitioner.text: Plan each level of the honours course to build towards the full set of threshold subject and generic skills by the end; in joint honours, expect part of the set to be met here and the rest supplied by the other subject.

forBeneficiary.text: As you move through each year of an honours degree you will build up, step by step, everything the threshold asks; if you study housing as a joint subject you will meet part of it here and add skills from your other subject.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Housing Studies degree

statements.about: fair recognition of prior learning and support for all
statements.paraphrase: Courses recognise prior learning and entrants arrive by many routes; at postgraduate level, RPL and course rules should not penalise those admitted on alternative or older experience, and support should be open to all students, for example study skills packages to ease the move into higher-level study.

forPractitioner.text: Write RPL and course regulations so that postgraduate entrants with alternative, equivalent or dated experience are not disadvantaged, and offer support such as study skills packages to every student.

forBeneficiary.text: If you join with work experience instead of the usual qualifications, the rules should not count against you, and you should be able to get support, such as help with study skills, regulations and difficulties.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Housing Studies degree

statements.appliesTo: courses and students seeking CIH chartered membership
statements.about: work experience for CIH chartered membership; employer partnerships
statements.paraphrase: Partnerships with housing organisations for work experience are core to undergraduate and postgraduate courses; CIH chartered membership accreditation requires set work experience in a housing role, and providers are expected to run employer groups that inform curriculum and skills.

forPractitioner.text: Build partnerships with housing employers to secure the prescribed work experience that CIH chartered membership requires; convene employer groups that meet regularly and invite partners to comment on curriculum and skills development.

forBeneficiary.text: If you are aiming for chartered membership of the Chartered Institute of Housing, you must complete set work experience in a housing role; your course works with employers to help you find it and to bring guest speakers and projects.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Housing Studies degree

statements.about: external reference points in monitoring and review
statements.paraphrase: Degree-awarding bodies monitor and periodically review their courses and will use external reference points, this statement among them, to keep their provision in line with sector norms.

forPractitioner.text: In monitoring and periodic review, use this statement among other external reference points to check that provision matches sector norms, and use monitoring data to understand achievement and plan ahead.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a quality assurance duty on the awarding body

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Housing Studies degree

statements.about: external reviewers confirm threshold standards
statements.paraphrase: Externality is essential to UK quality assurance: providers will bring in external reviewers during periodic review to give an outside view of changes and confirm that threshold standards are met and content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Include external reviewers in periodic review so that proposed changes get an outside view and threshold standards and subject content are confirmed.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a quality assurance duty on the provider

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Housing Studies degree

statements.about: CIH accreditation shapes content and change
statements.paraphrase: Courses may undergo internal monitoring, external review and CIH validation; where a course seeks CIH accreditation, the body's requirements shape the core content and skills it must deliver and the engagement with CIH that changes need.

forPractitioner.text: If the course seeks or holds CIH accreditation, deliver the content and skills the CIH requires and engage with the CIH, as it requires, before changing content or delivery.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition on accredited courses, met by the provider

statements.appliesTo: the teaching, learning and assessment strategy
statements.about: a strategy matched to outcomes; work-based learning where accredited
statements.paraphrase: A typical course's strategy makes plain why its methods suit the intended outcomes, is expected to use varied approaches that meet varied learning styles and needs, and, where the course is professionally accredited, will include work-based or work-related learning for newcomers and experienced staff alike.

forPractitioner.text: Make the fit between methods and intended outcomes explicit; use a variety of approaches for different learners; on an accredited course, include work-based or work-related learning for students new to housing and for those already in it.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect a mix of teaching and assessment that suits different ways of learning; on a professionally accredited course you will have chances to learn through or about work, whether you are new to housing or already work in it.

statements.appliesTo: the teaching, learning and assessment strategy
statements.about: student-centred strategy and recognition of prior learning
statements.paraphrase: The strategy is anticipated to be student-centred with review built in; learning, teaching and assessment are expected to recognise prior knowledge and experience and to clarify any exemption; practitioners may advise; alignment with EDI and ESD is encouraged.

forPractitioner.text: Keep the strategy student-centred and reviewed, recognise what students already know and have done, make exemption routes clear, involve housing practitioners where useful and align activities with EDI and ESD themes.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect your course to recognise what you already know from life and work, to make clear whether any part can be exempted and to build in equality, inclusion and sustainability.

statements.appliesTo: courses and institutions offering virtual and blended learning
statements.about: digital expectations, library support and the digital divide
statements.paraphrase: Courses should be supported by clear guidance on what digital technology students need (with training if required) and on using library resources; institutions with virtual or blended learning should be alert to the digital divide and arrange support.

forPractitioner.text: Tell students clearly what digital technology they need and offer training; support use of the library; where delivery is virtual or blended, plan for students on the wrong side of the digital divide and, where you can, point applicants to preparatory resources.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be told clearly what technology you need and offered training, shown how to use the library well and, if you study online or in a blended way, supported if you lack equipment or connection.

statements.about: a range of teaching approaches for different learners
statements.paraphrase: In both campus and online settings a range of teaching approaches is expected, to suit different learning styles; the examples given run from lectures and seminars to supervision, directed study, fieldwork with adjustments, problem-based learning and negotiated or work-related learning.

forPractitioner.text: Use several teaching approaches, for example lectures, small-group work, one-to-one supervision, directed study, site visits with reasonable adjustments, problem-based and team work, and negotiated or work-related learning that serves employability.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect a mix of teaching, such as lectures, seminars, supervision, guided study, site visits, problem-solving in teams and learning through work.

statements.about: accessible materials and clear module outcomes
statements.paraphrase: Materials are expected to be accessible to all and to give full, accurate course documentation, and each module's learning outcomes will be stated clearly and be achievable, with reading and other resources indicated.

forPractitioner.text: Provide accessible materials and complete, accurate documentation; for every module, state clear and achievable outcomes and indicate the reading and resources that support them.

forBeneficiary.text: You will be given clear, achievable outcomes for every module, with guidance on what to read, and accessible, accurate information about your course.

statements.about: alternative viewpoints, reflection and real-world challenges in diverse settings
statements.paraphrase: Teaching should open up alternative viewpoints, reflection on experience and real problems, and courses should use campuses, communities and online spaces as a living laboratory for topics from housing innovation to local governance, with digital tools to record and repeat the experience inclusively.

forPractitioner.text: Use teaching that surfaces alternative viewpoints, reflection and real-world challenges; treat campus, community and sector settings as a living laboratory and use digital tools to record and share that learning inclusively.

forBeneficiary.text: You should meet different viewpoints, reflect on experience and work on real housing challenges, often in the community, on campus or online.

statements.about: diverse voices, decolonisation and transformative learning
statements.paraphrase: Course design should widen literature and resources to include more voices, especially tenants and under-represented communities; historical approaches and the decolonisation of the curriculum should get careful thought; learning should change ways of thinking and practising and make students informed advocates of sustainable development; and courses should offer multi, inter and trans-disciplinary experiences beyond UK-centred practice.

forPractitioner.text: Broaden reading lists with tenant voices and under-represented communities, reconsider historical approaches and decolonise the curriculum, aim for learning that changes how students think and practise and give interdisciplinary experiences beyond UK-centred housing practice.

forBeneficiary.text: You should read and hear from a wider range of voices, including tenants and under-represented communities, question how housing history has been told and look beyond UK practice, so that you can speak up well for sustainable development.

statements.about: blended learning, group work and critical reflection
statements.paraphrase: Blended learning is increasingly likely; digital teaching can be used creatively and fairly for an inclusive, immersive experience, group work builds collaborative competencies and chances for critical reflection on one's own and others' views should be promoted.

forPractitioner.text: Use digital and blended methods creatively and equitably, set real problems and group tasks (online too) and promote critical reflection on students' own perspectives and those of others.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be given chances to reflect critically on your own views and those of others, often through group work and blended learning on real housing problems.

statements.appliesTo: the learning environment for housing studies
statements.about: interdisciplinary or transdisciplinary learning
statements.paraphrase: Housing studies education needs a learning environment that supports learning across disciplines.

forPractitioner.text: Provide learning that crosses disciplines, such as shared modules or joint projects.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition of the learning environment, provided by the course

statements.appliesTo: the learning environment for housing studies
statements.about: inclusive and accessible learning
statements.paraphrase: Housing studies education needs learning that includes everyone and that everyone can reach.

forPractitioner.text: Make every part of learning inclusive and accessible to all students.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition of the learning environment, provided by the course

statements.appliesTo: the learning environment for housing studies
statements.about: ESD underpinning learning
statements.paraphrase: Housing studies education needs education for sustainable development to sit beneath learning.

forPractitioner.text: Let sustainable development underpin learning across the course, not one module alone.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition of the learning environment, provided by the course

statements.appliesTo: the learning environment for housing studies
statements.about: extra and co-curricular opportunities
statements.paraphrase: Housing studies education needs extra-curricular and co-curricular opportunities that are offered and recognised.

forPractitioner.text: Offer and formally recognise extra and co-curricular opportunities.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition of the learning environment, provided by the course

statements.appliesTo: the learning environment for housing studies
statements.about: campus, outdoor and virtual spaces for ESD competencies
statements.paraphrase: Housing studies education needs campus, outdoor and virtual spaces to be used fully as alternative places to build and show ESD competencies.

forPractitioner.text: Use campus, outdoor and virtual spaces as settings in which students develop and show sustainability competencies.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition of the learning environment, provided by the course

statements.appliesTo: the learning environment for housing studies
statements.about: policies for synoptic assessment that connect modules
statements.paraphrase: Housing studies education needs policies that allow synoptic assessment, so students connect learning across modules and integrate it as they progress.

forPractitioner.text: Allow synoptic assessment in regulations so that students can link and integrate learning across modules as they progress.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition set by the course regulations

statements.about: clear, aligned aims, content and marking criteria
statements.paraphrase: Educators are encouraged to think creatively about assessment; a strategy for assessment and feedback helps students show their attainment and see their progress, and for each method the aims, content requirements and marking criteria should be clearly set out and aligned with the curriculum, teaching approaches and outcomes.

forPractitioner.text: For every assessment method, define aims, content requirements and marking criteria clearly and align them with the knowledge and skills taught, the teaching approaches and the course outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: For every assessment you should be told clearly what it is for, what it must contain and how it will be marked, and these should match what you were taught.

statements.about: accessible mixed assessment and published criteria
statements.paraphrase: Students should be able to show the full range of their abilities through a mix of assessment methods equally open to all backgrounds and situations; the means of assessment are expected to be documented and shared, and criteria published for all summative assessment.

forPractitioner.text: Offer varied assessment methods, each open on equal terms whatever students' educational background or circumstances, document and share how assessment works and publish criteria for every summative task.

forBeneficiary.text: You should have the chance to show everything you can do through a mix of assessments that work for students from any background, with the arrangements and marking criteria shared with you in advance.

statements.about: a diverse range of assessment methods with adjustments
statements.paraphrase: It is anticipated that varied assessment methods are used so that the whole range of housing knowledge, skills and standards is shown, with reasonable adjustments for disabled students where needed.

forPractitioner.text: Use a diverse range of methods so that every part of the knowledge, skills and standards can be evidenced, and make reasonable adjustments for disabled students.

forBeneficiary.text: You can expect several kinds of assessment, so that you can show the full range of what you know and can do, with adjustments if you are disabled.

statements.about: providers refer to Annex D for performance above threshold
statements.paraphrase: Most students will do well above the minimum; each provider sets its own way of judging the evidence and should refer to Annex D, which classifies honours outcomes at FHEQ Level 6 and FQHEIS Level 10 and describes the four honours classes.

forPractitioner.text: When deciding what evidence shows performance above the threshold, use your own method but refer to Annex D's descriptions of the 1st, 2:1, 2:2 and 3rd at FHEQ Level 6 and FQHEIS Level 10.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in setting classification evidence

statements.about: housing as a social determinant of well-being
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of why housing is a key social factor in the well-being of residents and communities.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically how housing shapes the well-being of residents and communities.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand in a systematic way how housing affects the well-being of the people and communities who live in it.

statements.about: state intervention and the changing production, consumption and experience of housing
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of why the state intervenes in housing markets and how producing, consuming and living in housing are changing.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically the case for state intervention in housing markets and how production, consumption and experience of housing change.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand why governments step into the housing market and how the way homes are built, bought, rented and lived in keeps changing.

statements.about: how housing problems emerge and the policy and legal responses
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of how housing problems arise and are recognised, and of how policy and law have developed to deal with them.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically how housing problems evolve and are identified and how policy and legal frameworks respond.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand how housing problems come about and are recognised, and how policy and the law have changed to tackle them.

statements.about: how housing policy is made and implemented
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of how housing policy is made and carried out locally and nationally, and how it connects with wider public policy.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically how local and national housing policy is formulated and put into effect and how it relates to wider public policy.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand how housing policy is made and put into practice locally and nationally, and how it links with other public policy.

statements.about: housing organisations and their governance
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of the different kinds of housing organisation, how each is governed and the difficulties governance faces.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically the forms of housing organisation, their governance and its challenges.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand the different types of housing organisation, how they are run and governed and what makes governing them hard.

statements.about: models of housing need and responsive systems
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of the different ways housing need is modelled and of building systems that respond to diverse individuals and groups.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically different models of housing need and how to develop systems that respond to diverse people and groups.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand the different ways of defining housing need and how to build systems that respond to many different people and groups.

statements.about: how housing bodies and professionals tackle wider social inequality
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of how housing organisations and practitioners can act on wider social inequalities at structural, institutional and individual level.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically how housing organisations and professionals can tackle social inequalities structurally, institutionally and individually.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand how housing organisations and the people who work in them can tackle wider social inequality at every level, from systems to individuals.

statements.about: comparative housing systems and transferring good practice
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of comparing housing systems and policies across the UK and beyond, finding and applying lessons and good practice where they fit.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically how to compare housing systems and policies within the UK and internationally and how to identify and apply learning and good practice.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand how to compare housing systems across the UK nations and other countries, and how to pick out and use lessons that work elsewhere.

statements.about: resident involvement and reaching seldom-heard groups
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of why involving residents in decisions helps and how to reach individuals and groups seldom heard because of barriers to taking part.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically the benefits of resident involvement in decisions and how to engage seldom-heard people and groups facing barriers.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand why it helps to involve residents in decisions and how to reach people and groups who are rarely heard because something stops them taking part.

statements.about: housing economics and finance
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of the core principles of housing economics and housing finance.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically the main principles of housing economics and finance.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand the main ideas of how housing economics and housing finance work.

statements.about: business planning, service management and delivery
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of the core principles of the business planning cycle and of managing and delivering services.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically the main principles of business planning, service management and service delivery.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand the main ideas behind business planning and how housing services are managed and delivered.

statements.about: choosing and applying research methods in housing
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of selecting and using suitable research methods and methodologies in a housing setting.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically how to identify and apply appropriate research methods and methodologies in housing contexts.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand how to choose the right research methods for a housing question and how to use them.

statements.about: evidence-based solutions to housing issues
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of how to find solutions to housing issues that rest on evidence.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically how to identify solutions to housing issues grounded in evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand how to find answers to housing issues that are backed by evidence.

statements.about: presenting information, data and concepts to varied audiences
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of presenting information, data and ideas to different audiences.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically how to put information, data and concepts across to different audiences.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand how to present information, data and ideas to different kinds of audience.

statements.about: leadership and management in housing organisations
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of the core principles of leading and managing in housing and how to apply them in housing organisations.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically the key principles of housing leadership and management and their application in housing organisations.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand the main ideas of leadership and management in housing and how they are used in housing organisations.

statements.about: environmental sustainability and the climate crisis in housing
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of aspects of environmental sustainability, including how the climate crisis bears on designing, developing, maintaining and managing housing.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically aspects of environmental sustainability, including the climate crisis's impact across the design, development, maintenance and management of housing.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand environmental sustainability in housing, including how the climate crisis affects the way homes are designed, built, maintained and managed.

statements.about: renewal, refurbishment and regeneration with resident engagement
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of the core principles of renewing, refurbishing and regenerating housing, involving residents in these processes and reaching fair outcomes.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically the principles of housing renewal, refurbishment and regeneration, resident engagement in them and equitable outcomes.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand the main ideas of renewing, refurbishing and regenerating housing, how to involve residents and how to make the results fair.

statements.about: the causes of tenure-related stigma
statements.paraphrase: Will have systematic understanding of analysing what leads to stigma attached to housing tenure.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, graduates understand systematically how to analyse the factors behind tenure-related stigma.

forBeneficiary.text: To reach the threshold for an honours degree, you will understand how to analyse why people are stigmatised because of the kind of housing tenure they live in.

statements.about: CIH specification met in full on accredited courses
statements.paraphrase: On accredited courses, the requirements of the CIH specification are to be met in full, as part of the threshold.

forPractitioner.text: If the course is accredited by the CIH, make sure every requirement of its specification is fully met.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on accredited courses, not an understanding the student shows

statements.about: typical rung set by providers' marking schemes
statements.paraphrase: Criteria for achievement above the threshold at 2:1 and 2:2 will follow each provider's common or generic undergraduate marking scheme; the statement lists no typical items.

forPractitioner.text: Judge 2:1 and 2:2 work against your institution's common or generic undergraduate marking scheme; the statement gives no subject list for this rung.

forBeneficiary.text: For a 2:1 or a 2:2 you will be judged against your university's own marking scheme, which goes beyond the threshold.

statements.about: excellent rung set by providers' marking schemes
statements.paraphrase: Criteria for excellent, first-class achievement will follow each provider's common or generic undergraduate marking scheme; the statement lists no excellent items.

forPractitioner.text: Judge first-class work against your institution's common or generic undergraduate marking scheme; the statement gives no subject list for this rung.

forBeneficiary.text: For a first you will be judged against your university's own marking scheme for excellent work.

headingPath: Master's level degrees in Housing Studies

statements.about: evaluating current research and advanced scholarship
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to judge current research and advanced scholarship.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates evaluate current research and advanced scholarship critically.

forBeneficiary.text: For a master's you will be able to judge the quality and value of current research and advanced scholarship.

headingPath: Master's level degrees in Housing Studies

statements.about: how research advances knowledge
statements.paraphrase: Will understand the ways research moves knowledge forward.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates understand how research advances knowledge.

forBeneficiary.text: For a master's you will understand how research moves knowledge forward.

headingPath: Master's level degrees in Housing Studies

statements.about: the limits of current knowledge
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to recognise where present knowledge stops.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates identify where the limits of current knowledge lie.

forBeneficiary.text: For a master's you will be able to see where current knowledge in housing runs out.

headingPath: Master's level degrees in Housing Studies

statements.about: creating new insight in the field
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to produce new insight in the field.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates create new insights in housing studies.

forBeneficiary.text: For a master's you will be able to produce new insight in housing studies.

headingPath: Master's level degrees in Housing Studies

statements.about: understanding of housing knowledge much of it at the forefront of research and practice
statements.paraphrase: Will have shown understanding of the housing knowledge set out for the honours threshold, much of it at the leading edge of scholarship and professional practice.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates show understanding of the housing knowledge in the undergraduate threshold, with much of it reaching the forefront of research and of practice.

forBeneficiary.text: For a master's in housing you will show you understand the knowledge set for the honours degree, much of it at the leading edge of research and professional practice.

headingPath: Master's level degrees in Housing Studies

statements.about: higher-level skills at the FHEQ Level 7 and FQHEIS Level 11 descriptor
statements.paraphrase: Higher-level skills grow through self-directed academic and professional development, and master's students are expected to achieve to the descriptor for a qualification at FHEQ Level 7 and SCQF Level 11 on the FQHEIS.

forPractitioner.text: Develop master's students' higher-level skills through self-directed academic and professional work, and set master's outcomes against the FHEQ Level 7 (FQHEIS Level 11) qualification descriptor.

forBeneficiary.text: On a master's course you will build higher-level skills largely by directing your own academic and professional development, to the level set for master's qualifications across the UK.

statements.about: independent and joint work on complex problems and synthesis of knowledge
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to work alone and with others to find complex problems and draw together what is known on a subject or topic.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will work alone and in teams to pinpoint complex problems and synthesise the current state of knowledge on a subject or topic.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to work on your own and with others to spot complex problems and pull together what is already known about a topic.

statements.about: ownership of learning, judgement and communicating ideas
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to own their learning, show conceptual understanding, judge soundly and communicate ideas well to varied audiences.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will take personal responsibility for their learning, show conceptual understanding, make sound judgements and communicate ideas effectively to different audiences.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to take charge of your learning, show you grasp the ideas, make sound judgements and explain your ideas well to different people.

statements.about: collaboration across disciplines in assessed and other activities
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to work with others in assessed and unassessed activities, including people from other disciplines, as the inter-professional nature of housing work demands.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will collaborate in assessed and non-assessed activities, including with other disciplines, mirroring the inter-professional character of housing practice.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to work with others, including people from other professions, in assessed and unassessed tasks, as you will in housing work.

statements.about: awareness of and professional responsibility for equality, diversity and inclusion
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to show awareness of equality, diversity and inclusion issues and take professional responsibility for dealing with them.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will show awareness of equality, diversity and inclusion issues and accept professional responsibility for addressing them.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to show that you understand issues of equality, diversity and inclusion and that you take professional responsibility for acting on them.

statements.about: using ICT to gather and evaluate information and data
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to use various information and communications technology packages to collect and judge information and data from many sources.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will use a range of ICT packages to gather and weigh information and data from varied sources.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to use a range of software to gather and assess information and data from different sources.

statements.about: identifying housing problems, sustainability included, and alternative solutions
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to recognise housing problems, environmental and sustainability ones among them, and devise other possible solutions.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will identify housing problems, environmental and sustainability ones among them, and devise alternative solutions.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to spot housing problems, including environmental and sustainability ones, and come up with different ways to solve them.

statements.about: reflecting on and managing learning, development and ethical practice
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to reflect on and direct their own learning and personal development and their ethical and professional practice.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will reflect on and direct their own learning, personal development and ethical, professional practice.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to reflect on and manage your own learning and personal growth, and how you act ethically and professionally.

statements.about: using learning for employability and entrepreneurship
statements.paraphrase: Will be able to reflect deliberately on their learning and use it to improve employability and entrepreneurship in line with the career they want.

forPractitioner.text: Graduates will consciously reflect on and use their learning to strengthen their employability and entrepreneurship for the career they intend.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree, you will be able to think about what you have learned and use it to make yourself more employable and enterprising for the career you want.
